string-array.name: ScamTypesDESC
string-array.item: A scammer calls you with a sales pitch for renewing your auto warranty or insurance policy. The scammer may have acquired information about your car and its existing warranty to make the offer seem more credible. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Scammers pretend to be your bank through calls, texts, or emails, often claiming there\'s suspicious activity on your account. They use urgency to trick you into sharing personal or financial information, sending money, or transferring funds to a so-called "safe" account. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Scammers open by asking a yes-or-no question, such as: "Can you hear me?" or "Is this X?" Their goal is to record you saying "yes" in response. They then may use that recording to authorize charges over the phone. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)
Scammers call asking for charitable donations, often after large-scale disasters. They may make up phony charities or spoof a real charity to trick you out of your money. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)
Scammers may try and provide a discount on a product, often too-good-to-be-true. Rather than answer, check that the discount is legit.

Scammers sometimes prey on grandparents by claiming their family members are in jail or in trouble and need money quickly. They use stolen personal information such as family member names and hometowns to seem more convincing. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Scammers often pose as government entities, Medicare representatives, or insurance providers. They may offer free health screenings, gifts, lower premiums, or special enrollment deals. Their real goal is to steal personal information and money. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Callers posing as government officials, often from the Social Security Administration, claim that you\'ve been a victim of identity theft. These scammers ask for personal information or payment of some kind, or access to your bank account. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Scammers spoof caller ID information that displays the same initial digits as your own phone number (usually the first six), making it seem like someone else with a local number is trying to reach you. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)
Scammers might try and get information from people by pretending to be a company or person you know. This is a common scam tactic over text and email as well.
Around the time of elections, scam and spam calls surrounding elections tend to increase. They will try and get you to vote for a specific politician.

If you\'ve already fallen for a scam, another scammer may call you and offer to get you your money back for a fee. Their goal is to double dip and steal more of your money. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Scammers may pose as government officials, often from the Social Security Administration, to request your Social Security Number or a payment of some sort. Sometimes, they claim your SSN is suspended. The call may spoof what appears to be a legitimate Social Security Administration number. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

Phone scammers may masquerade as tech support employees for a major company in order to take your money or install a virus on your computer. They may call from what seem to be legitimate company numbers using caller ID spoofing. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)
Scam callers leave voicemails threatening legal action if you don\'t call back. Our guidance is: Never call back an unfamiliar number, because it may lead to a scam. (From fcc.gov/scam-glossary)

item.name: How To Recognize a Phone Scam

string-array.item:
There is no prize
Be careful if someone tells you that you won a prize but asks you to pay a fee to receive it.

You won\’t be arrested
Scammers may pretend to be law enforcement and threaten to arrest you unless you pay immediately.

You don\’t need to decide now
Be suspicious of callers who pressure you to make an immediate decision. Take your time to verify their claims.

Only scammers demand you pay certain ways
Scammers will often insist you pay in a way that makes it hard to get your money back — by wire transfer , gift card, cryptocurrency, or payment app. Anyone who insists that you can only pay that way is a scammer.

Government agencies won\’t call to confirm your sensitive information
Don\'t share your Social Security number or other sensitive information with unexpected callers claiming to represent government agencies.

You shouldn’t be getting all those calls
Be cautious of unwanted sales calls and illegal robocalls. They may be scams.

(From fcc.gov/phone scam)

Impersonator Scams
Scammers pretend to be government officials, family members, or trusted businesses. They may use fake names or caller IDs to appear legitimate. Always verify their identity before sharing information or sending money.

Debt Relief and Credit Repair Scams
Scammers promise to lower your interest rates, fix your credit, or forgive student loans in exchange for an upfront fee. Be cautious of these promises and research the company first.

Business and Investment Scams
Scammers promise business opportunities or guaranteed investment profits, including cryptocurrency returns. Be suspicious of guaranteed profits and research investments before paying.

Charity Scams
Scammers pretend to represent real charities and ask for donations, often after disasters. Check the charity before donating, and never feel pressured to give immediately.

Extended Car Warranty Scams
Scammers use information about your car to sell overpriced or fake extended warranties. Research the company and contract before making a payment.

Free Trial Scams
Scammers offer free trials but may enroll you in recurring payments. Read the terms carefully and check your billing statements for unexpected charges.

Loan Scams
Scammers promise guaranteed loans or credit cards but demand an upfront fee. Be careful because legitimate lenders generally do not guarantee approval in this way.

Prize and Lottery Scams
Scammers claim you have won a prize but ask you to pay taxes or fees to receive it. Remember, you should not have to pay to collect a prize.

Travel and Timeshare Scams
Scammers offer free or cheap vacations but demand fees upfront. Others promise to sell your timeshare for a fee but may never find a buyer. Research the company before paying.

(From fcc.gov/phone scam)

item.name: How To Stop Calls From Scammers

string-array.item:
Hang Up
If you receive a suspicious call or robocall, hang up. Do not press any numbers to speak to an operator or remove yourself from the call list, as this may lead to more unwanted calls.

Use Call Blocking
Call-blocking and call-labeling services can help reduce unwanted calls. Check what services your phone carrier offers or look for trusted call-blocking apps.

Do Not Trust Caller ID
Scammers can fake the name or number displayed on your caller ID. Even if a call appears to come from a government agency or a local number, it could be a scam. Verify the caller before sharing personal information.

(From fcc.gov/phone scam)

item.name: What To Do If You Already Paid a Scammer

string-array.item:
Stop Sending Money
Scammers may ask you to pay using gift cards, cryptocurrency, payment apps, or wire transfers. These payment methods can be difficult to reverse. Never send more money if someone pressures you to pay this way.

Contact Your Bank or Payment Provider
If you already paid, contact your bank, credit card company, gift card provider, or payment app immediately. Report the transaction as fraudulent and ask if the payment can be reversed or refunded.

Keep Your Payment Records
Save receipts, transaction details, messages, and other evidence. These records may help when reporting the scam and requesting a refund.

Protect Your Personal Information
If you shared your Social Security number, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance. If you shared your password, change it immediately and update it on other accounts where you used the same password.

Watch Out for Recovery Scams
Be careful of people who promise to recover your lost money for a fee. They may be scammers trying to steal even more money or personal information.

(From fcc.gov/phone scam)

Report Scams That Caused Financial Loss
If you lost money or have information about a phone scammer, report it to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

Report Unwanted Calls
If you received a suspicious or unwanted call but did not lose money, report it at DoNotCall.gov.

Provide Call Details
Include the caller\'s phone number, the number displayed on your caller ID, the date and time of the call, and any callback number provided. This information helps the FTC track scammers and supports call-blocking efforts.

(From fcc.gov/phone scam)
